title: Voters oust key state incumbents in rare primary shakeup, sending warning to officeholders
text:
In a year when Utah voters largely rewarded federal incumbents, they delivered a sharp rebuke at the state level, ousting powerful figures including Senate Pres
FILE - A plan to put Utah income tax cuts on autopilot narrowly advanced at the Utah State Capitol. In a year when Utah voters largely rewarded federal incumbents, they delivered a sharp rebuke at the state level, ousting powerful figures including Senate President Stuart Adams and other longtime lawmakers in Tuesday's primary election.
The results highlighted a tale of two elections: stability and moderation on the federal side, but significant turnover driven by local frustrations over issues like data centers, water resources and long-simmering controversies, according to political analyst Jason Perry of the Hinckley Institute of Politics at the University of Utah.
"It's a very interesting tale of two different kinds of results on the federal level and on the state level," Perry told KUTV 2 anchor Heidi Hatch on Wednesday. "We saw a lot of people rewarding incumbents on the federal side. Definitely not the case when it comes to the state level elections and big changes happen that are going to impact the state of Utah for the foreseeable future.
"Celeste Maloy wins Republican nomination for US House in Utah's 3rd Congressional District Incumbents prevailed in congressional contests, including Rep. Blake Moore, who fended off a challenge from former state Rep. Karianne Lisonbee. In the newly drawn 1st Congressional District, former Rep.
Ben McAdams won the Democratic primary.
"Phil Lyman, for example, showed that for sort of an anti-establishment candidate, there is a certain number of votes that you're going to get," he said. "But if you look at that particular race, you look even with Ben McAdams, you saw one side or other of the middle, more of a centrist approach in the state of Utah.
"Adams, one of the state's most powerful Republicans, conceded his race in Senate District 7 to Fruit Heights attorney Stephanie Hollist less than two hours after polls closed. Other incumbents, including Sen. Dan McCay and Trevor Lee, also lost. Utah voters have historically been reluctant to unseat incumbents, but Perry said specific, timely issues mobilized voters this cycle.
"Voters were very much paying attention. And there were very specific things happening at a very specific time," he said, citing concerns over data centers' impact on water, power and air quality.
"These became very specific issues that Utahns, particularly in those areas, were looking at. ""I think that's certainly top of mind and it is a key political elected official, particularly I would say the most powerful in the state of Utah," Perry said of Adams' role on the MIDA board and data center issues. "It just happens in public office for long have enough issues come forward and the issues just start getting heavier and heavier over time.
" He added that an accumulation of concerns, including past legislative actions, combined with strong voter mobilization created "the perfect confluence of issues and concern. " McCay faced discontent over issues including the state flag change and other positions accumulated over years in office, Perry said. "There was a record that voters looked at with Dan McKay, and that's what we saw in the results.
""If you say I'm a loud conservative and I have a lot of negative things to say as part of my conservatism, that clearly is not what is resonating with voters," he said. "All elected officials should look at this primary and realize there's no huge amount of deference that just comes to being the incumbent," he said. "People are paying attention in a very real way to issues that they care about the most.
"He pointed to backlash against Box Elder County commissioners over data center issues as further evidence. Voters showed a high level of distrust in the establishment, Perry said, which amplified specific grievances.
"If you have voters that are sort of not trusting the institutions and you add these very personal issues on top of that, you start seeing people in Utah willing and maybe even motivated to make a change. "Perry said the primary results underscore that voters won't be taken for granted. "We have a certain party we identify with but you can't take me for granted — there are some issues that will topple my support," he said.
Turnout appeared typical for a midterm primary, around 30% range, with standard voter motivation rather than a surge of younger participants.
"This primary has truly shown that there are issues that can resonate and there are issues that motivate people to get involved," he said. "I know from the conversations I've had with elected officials, they are watching and they are listening. And I think that's a good position for all of us.
